chunks.heading: Naming the sides of a right triangle
chunks.body: In a right triangle, label an angle. The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite is across from the angle, and adjacent is next to it.
chunks.checkText: In a right triangle, which side is always the longest?

chunks.heading: The sine ratio
chunks.body: Sine of an angle is opposite over hypotenuse: sin(A) = opposite / hypotenuse. It compares two sides of a [[mathadv-triangle-side-names|right triangle]].

chunks.heading: The cosine ratio
chunks.body: Cosine of an angle is adjacent over hypotenuse: cos(A) = adjacent / hypotenuse.
chunks.checkText: cos(A) equals...

chunks.heading: The tangent ratio
chunks.body: Tangent of an angle is opposite over adjacent: tan(A) = opposite / adjacent. You can also get it by dividing [[mathadv-sine-ratio|sin(A)]] by [[mathadv-cosine-ratio|cos(A)]].
chunks.checkText: tan(A) equals...

chunks.heading: Three more ratios: flip them over
chunks.body: Cosec, sec and cot are the flipped versions of [[mathadv-sine-ratio|sine]], [[mathadv-cosine-ratio|cosine]] and [[mathadv-tangent-ratio|tangent]]: cosec(A) = 1/sin(A), sec(A) = 1/cos(A), cot(A) = 1/tan(A).
chunks.checkText: sec(A) is the reciprocal of...

chunks.heading: Exact values for 30°, 45°, 60°
chunks.body: Some angles give exact trig values instead of decimals, like sin(30°) = 1/2 and cos(45°) = 1/sqrt(2). These come from two special triangles and are worth memorising.
chunks.checkText: sin(30°) equals exactly...

chunks.heading: Finding a missing side
chunks.body: To find an unknown side, write unknown/known = sin, cos or tan of the angle, then solve. Choose whichever ratio uses the sides you know from [[mathadv-triangle-side-names|the triangle]].
chunks.checkText: To find an unknown side, you set up an equation using...

checkOptions.text: The angle and one known side

chunks.heading: Finding a missing angle
chunks.body: If you know two sides, use the inverse of [[mathadv-sine-ratio|sin]], [[mathadv-cosine-ratio|cos]] or [[mathadv-tangent-ratio|tan]] on your calculator to find the angle.
chunks.checkText: To find an unknown angle from two known sides, you use...

chunks.heading: Looking up and looking down
chunks.body: The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to something above you. The angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal to something below you.
chunks.checkText: The angle of elevation is always measured from...

chunks.heading: Compass bearings
chunks.body: A compass bearing gives a direction as an angle turned from north or south, towards east or west, like N30°E or S45°W.
chunks.checkText: A compass bearing like N30°E is measured starting from...

chunks.heading: True bearings
chunks.body: A true bearing measures the angle clockwise from north, using three digits, like 030°T or 225°T. It's a different way to describe the same directions as a [[mathadv-compass-bearings|compass bearing]].
chunks.checkText: A true bearing is always measured...

chunks.heading: Trigonometry in 3D
chunks.body: For 3D shapes, sketch the situation, spot every triangle hiding inside it, mark the right angles, then solve one triangle at a time using [[mathadv-sine-ratio|sin]], [[mathadv-cosine-ratio|cos]] or [[mathadv-tangent-ratio|tan]].
chunks.checkText: The first step in a 3D trigonometry problem is to...

checkOptions.text: Sketch the situation and find the triangles

chunks.heading: The angle between a line and a flat surface
chunks.body: To find the angle between a line and a plane, drop a perpendicular from a point on the line down to the plane, then use the triangle this forms.
chunks.checkText: To measure the angle between a line and a plane, you first...

checkOptions.text: Drop a perpendicular onto the plane

chunks.heading: The angle between two flat surfaces
chunks.body: Two planes meet along a line. To find the angle between them, draw a line in each plane that is perpendicular to that meeting line, at the same point.
chunks.checkText: The angle between two planes is measured using lines that are...

checkOptions.text: Perpendicular to where the planes meet
Parallel to where the planes meet
Along the outer edges of each plane

chunks.heading: Angles beyond the triangle
chunks.body: A general angle is measured by rotating a ray from the positive x-axis. Rotating anticlockwise gives a positive angle; rotating clockwise gives a negative angle.
chunks.checkText: Rotating a ray clockwise from the positive x-axis gives a...

chunks.heading: Many angles, one ray
chunks.body: The same ray can represent many different [[mathadv-general-angle-ray|general angles]], because adding or subtracting 360° any number of times brings you back to the same ray.
chunks.checkText: Two angles that point to the same ray always differ by a multiple of...

chunks.heading: Redefining sin, cos and tan for any angle
chunks.body: Place the ray's endpoint at (x, y) on a circle of radius r. Then sin(A) = y/r, cos(A) = x/r and tan(A) = y/x, matching the [[mathadv-sine-ratio|old right-triangle definitions]] for acute angles.
chunks.checkText: For a general angle, cos(A) is defined as...

chunks.heading: The four quadrants
chunks.body: The coordinate plane is split into four quadrants, numbered 1 to 4 anticlockwise starting from the top right. Which quadrant a ray lies in affects the sign of its trig values.
chunks.checkText: The quadrants are numbered starting from...

chunks.heading: Remembering the signs: ASTC
chunks.body: In quadrant 1 All ratios are positive, in quadrant 2 only Sine is, in quadrant 3 only Tangent is, and in quadrant 4 only Cosine is. Remember it as 'All Stations To Central'.
chunks.checkText: In quadrant 3, which trig ratio is positive?

chunks.heading: The related acute angle
chunks.body: The related acute angle is the acute angle between a ray and the x-axis. Any angle has the same trig values as its related acute angle, apart from the sign.
chunks.checkText: The related acute angle is always measured between a ray and the...

chunks.heading: Working out any trig value
chunks.body: To evaluate a trig function for any angle: find its [[mathadv-related-acute-angle|related acute angle]], then use the [[mathadv-astc-rule|ASTC rule]] to decide if the answer is positive or negative.
chunks.checkText: To evaluate sin(150°) exactly, you first find...

checkOptions.text: The related acute angle, then check the sign

chunks.heading: Given one ratio, find the rest
chunks.body: If you know one trig ratio, sketch the ray on a circle, use Pythagoras' theorem to find the missing side, then use the [[mathadv-astc-rule|ASTC rule]] for the correct sign.
chunks.checkText: If sin(A) = 1/5, to find cos(A) you would use...

checkOptions.text: Pythagoras' theorem and the ASTC rule

chunks.heading: What is a radian?
chunks.body: An angle's size in radians is a ratio: the arc length it cuts off on a circle, divided by the radius of that circle. It's just a number, with no units.
chunks.checkText: An angle in radians is calculated as...

chunks.heading: A full turn in radians
chunks.body: One full revolution (360°) equals 2π radians, because the whole circumference divided by the radius is 2π.
chunks.checkText: 360° is equal to how many radians?

chunks.heading: A straight angle in radians
chunks.body: A straight angle (180°) equals π radians. This is half of the [[mathadv-full-turn-radians|full turn of 2π]].
chunks.checkText: 180° is equal to...

chunks.heading: A right angle in radians
chunks.body: A right angle (90°) equals π/2 radians — half of the [[mathadv-straight-angle-radians|straight angle of π]].
chunks.checkText: 90° is equal to...

chunks.heading: Converting degrees to radians
chunks.body: To turn degrees into radians, multiply by π/180. For example, 60° × π/180 = π/3 radians.
chunks.checkText: To convert degrees to radians, you multiply by...

chunks.heading: Converting radians to degrees
chunks.body: To turn radians into degrees, multiply by 180/π. For example, π/3 × 180/π = 60°.
chunks.checkText: To convert radians to degrees, you multiply by...

chunks.heading: How big is one radian?
chunks.body: One radian is about 57°, a bit less than a right angle. It's the angle where the arc length exactly equals the radius.

chunks.heading: Special angles in radians
chunks.body: The special angles convert simply: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, and 60° = π/3. These are worth memorising alongside the [[mathadv-special-angle-values|exact trig values]] for them.

chunks.heading: Set your calculator carefully
chunks.body: Before using trig functions with radians, always switch your calculator to radian mode. Forgetting this gives completely wrong answers.
chunks.checkText: Before evaluating sin(1) in radians, you should first...

checkOptions.text: Check the calculator is in radian mode

chunks.heading: The arc length formula
chunks.body: The length of an arc is l = rθ, where r is the radius and θ is the angle in [[mathadv-radian-definition|radians]] at the centre.
chunks.checkText: The formula for arc length is...

chunks.heading: The sector area formula
chunks.body: The area of a sector is A = (1/2)r^2θ, where θ is the angle in [[mathadv-radian-definition|radians]] at the centre of the circle.
chunks.checkText: The formula for the area of a sector is...

chunks.heading: Minor and major arcs
chunks.body: Two radii split a circle into two arcs. The minor arc is the shorter one, and the major arc is the longer one that goes the rest of the way around.
chunks.checkText: The minor arc of a circle is always the...

checkOptions.text: Straight line between the two points

chunks.heading: The area of a segment
chunks.body: A chord splits a circle into two segments. To find a segment's area, take the sector area and add or subtract the triangle area formed by the two radii and the chord.
